title: Genesis 45. The Cup of Revelation.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 45. The Cup of Revelation.
Then Joseph could not control himself before all who stood by him.
He could not control himself.
The man who controlled every test, the silver in the sacks,
the cup in Benjamin's grain, the seating by birthright, the five portions,
the harsh words, the interpreter, the mask, cannot control himself anymore.
The vessel that held the tears behind three closed doors,
the door of chapter forty-two, the door of chapter forty-three,
the door of chapter forty four, shatters.
Every wall Joseph built between his grief and his brothers collapses in one moment.
The Cup of testing, the Cup of yielding, the Cup of decision,
all of them, pour out at once.
He cried out: Cause everyone to go out from me!
No one else stood with him while Joseph made himself known to his brothers.
Everyone leaves.
The Egyptians.
The servants.
The interpreters.
The stewards.
The entire apparatus of power and disguise and control,
emptied from the room.
The man who wore Egyptian robes and bore an Egyptian name and spoke through an interpreter stands alone with the men who sold him.
The mask comes off.
The Cup is about to be poured.
He wept aloud.
The Egyptians heard.
And the house of Pharaoh heard.
The third weeping.
And the loudest.
Chapter forty-two: he wept at hearing their guilt, turned away, returned.
Chapter forty-three: he wept at seeing Benjamin, went to his room,
washed his face.
Chapter forty-five: he weeps so loud the nation hears.
The weeping has been building.
Each time more uncontrollable.
Each time closer to the surface.
Now it breaks through every boundary, private, public, national.
The Cup that held tears behind closed doors overflows into the open.
The weeping that was hidden is now heard by Pharaoh himself.
Joseph said to his brothers: I am Joseph.
Does my father still live?
I am Joseph.
The recognition pattern completes.
Chapter forty-two: Joseph recognized them; they did not recognize him.
Chapter forty-four: Judah recognized his own guilt.
Now Joseph makes himself known.
The one who was hidden, behind Egyptian clothes, behind a foreign name,
behind the office of power,
behind the mask of a governor who divines with cups, speaks.
The recognition that was used for deception in three generations,
Jacob deceiving Isaac, the brothers deceiving Jacob, Tamar deceiving Judah,
is now used for reconciliation.
The verb that meant lying is now meaning truth.
His brothers could not answer him,
for they were terrified at his presence.
terrified.
Disoriented.
The ones who sold him stand before the one they sold.
He has all, power.
They have no defense.
The Cup of decision was answered by Judah's willingness to stay.
Now the Cup overflows with revelation, and they cannot speak.
The brother they thought was dead is alive.
The brother they sold is the man they have been bowing to.
The brother they stripped is the man who has been clothing them.
The brother they threw into a pit is the man who controls all the grain in the world.
Joseph said to his brothers: Come near to me, please.
They came near.
Come near.
The same word used when God said to Moses:
do not come near, at the burning bush.
But here: come near.
The brother who was far, twenty-two years far, a pit far,
a prison far, a disguise far, says: come near.
The distance that was maintained by the mask is now closed by the voice.
The Cup that was held at arm's length is now offered at the table.
He said: I am Joseph your brother, whom you sold into Egypt.
Whom you sold, he names it.
He does not say: whom you lost.
Whom you thought was torn by wild animals.
Whom you reported missing, he says: whom you sold.
The word is, you sold.
The same word Judah used in chapter thirty-seven: come,
let us sell him to the Ishmaelites.
The same word the Midianites fulfilled:
they sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty shekels of silver.
Joseph speaks the exact word that described what they did.
He does not soften it.
He does not erase it.
He names the betrayal before he reframes it.
But now,
do not be grieved or angry with yourselves because you sold me here.
For God sent me before you to preserve life.
Do not be grieved.
The same Joseph who wept when he heard them say we are guilty now says:
do not be grieved.
The Cup of guilt that was opened in chapter forty-two is now being closed.
Not by denial, Joseph just named the sale.
Not by excuse, he does not say it was not that bad.
By reframing: God sent me before you to preserve life.
They sold him.
God sent him.
The same event.
Two truths.
Neither canceling the other.
The Cup of betrayal and the Cup of preservation are the same Cup,
seen from different ends.
The brothers held it as a cup of guilt.
Joseph holds it as a cup of providence.
Both are real.
The betrayal was real.
The guilt was real.
Judah's confession was real.
And God's purpose was working through the real betrayal.
Joseph does not say: you didn't really do it.
He says: you did it, and God used it.
For two years now there has been famine in the land.
And there are yet five years in which there will be no plowing and no harvest.
God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant on earth,
and to save you alive by a great deliverance.
A remnant.
A great deliverance.
The words that will echo through the rest of Scripture,
the remnant preserved, the deliverance provided.
The Cup that was carried into Egypt by force is now the Cup that preserves the covenant family from starvation.
The promise that was spoken to Abraham,
I will make you a great nation,
would have died in Canaan if Joseph had not been in Egypt.
The betrayal that was meant for harm became the means of survival.
The pit became the palace.
The prison became the storehouse.
The coat that was stripped became the robes that now clothe the brothers.
So now it was not you who sent me here, but God.
Not you who sent me.
But God.
Joseph does not erase the brothers' action.
He reframes it.
They sold.
God sent.
The same event.
Two agents.
One human, the sale.
One divine, the purpose.
Joseph sees both simultaneously.
The Cup holds both:
the bitterness of what they did and the providence of what God was doing through it.
Neither cancels the other.
The betrayal was real.
The providence was real.
And the providence does not excuse the betrayal, it redeems it.
He has made me a father to Pharaoh,
lord of all his house,
and ruler over all the land of Egypt.
A father to Pharaoh.
The slave became a father.
The prisoner became a lord.
The forgotten became a ruler.
The boy who was the youngest at the table,
the son of the favorite wife,
is now a father to the most powerful man on earth.
The Cup that was held by a child is now held by a patriarch.
Hurry, and go up to my father, and tell him:
This is what your son Joseph says:
God has made me lord of all Egypt.
Come down to me.
Do not wait.
Do not wait.
The same urgency as Jacob's dream at Bethel, arise, go up.
Now Joseph says: come down.
The father who sent his son to check on his brothers will now be invited to come to the son.
The man who said go and see the welfare of your brothers will now be told:
your son is alive, come and see.
You shall dwell in the land of Goshen.
You will be near to me, you, your children, your children's children,
your flocks, your herds, and all that you have.
There I will provide for you,
for there are yet five years of famine,
lest you come to poverty, you, and your household,
and all that you have.
Goshen.
The land that will become the setting for Israel's growth from a family into a nation.
The land that will become the place of bondage four hundred years later.
The land where the covenant family will multiply until they are too many to be ignored and too foreign to be accepted.
The descent that will become enslavement begins as an invitation to provision.
The Cup that carries the covenant into Egypt begins as a cup of grace,
Come.
Dwell.
I will provide.
He fell on his brother Benjamin's neck and wept.
And Benjamin wept on his neck.
The neck-embrace.
The same phrase used in chapter thirty-three,
when Esau fell on Jacob's neck and kissed him.
The neck-embrace of reconciliation.
Now Joseph and Benjamin, the two sons of Rachel,
weep on each other's necks.
The mother who died on the road to Bethlehem,
who named her first son add and her second son,
son of my sorrow,
is represented by two sons weeping in each other's arms.
The Cup that Rachel's death emptied is now refilled by her sons' tears.
He kissed all his brothers and wept on them.
After that, his brothers talked with him.
He kissed all his brothers.
Not just Benjamin.
All of them.
The ten who sold him.
The ones who stripped his coat.
The ones who sat to eat while he was in the pit.
The ones who dipped the coat in blood and lied to their father.
He kissed them.
The Cup of testing, the Cup of yielding, the Cup of decision,
becomes the Cup of communion.
They talked.
Face to face.
Brother to brother.
For the first time in twenty-two years.
The mask is gone.
The interpreter is gone.
The silver cup is gone.
Only the brothers remain.
And the tears.
And the words.
The report of it was heard in Pharaoh's house, saying:
Joseph's brothers have come.
It pleased Pharaoh well, and his servants.
Pharaoh is pleased.
The pagan king who said can we find a man like this,
in whom is the Spirit of God?
is pleased that the man's family has arrived.
The Cup that blessed Potiphar's house now blesses Pharaoh's house.
The covenant that was carried by one man into Egypt now brings an entire household.
The blessing of Abraham,
in you all families of the earth shall be blessed,
continues to flow through Joseph to the nation that holds him.
Pharaoh said: Tell your brothers to do this:
Load your animals and go to the land of Canaan.
Take your father and your households and come to me.
And I will give you the good of the land of Egypt.
You will eat the fat of the land.
Do not concern yourselves about your belongings,
for the good of all the land of Egypt is yours.
The pagan king gives the covenant family the best of his land.
The same pattern as Melchizedek blessing Abraham.
The same pattern as Abimelech recognizing Isaac.
The outsider sees what the covenant carries and responds with generosity.
Pharaoh, the most powerful man on earth,
gives land to a family of shepherds because one of those shepherds saved his nation.
The sons of Israel did so.
Joseph gave them wagons, according to the commandment of Pharaoh,
and gave them provision for the way.
He gave each one of them changes of clothing,
but to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver and five changes of clothing.
Changes of clothing.
The garment pattern comes full circle.
The coat that was stripped by brothers in chapter thirty-seven.
The garment that was grabbed by a wife in chapter thirty-nine.
The prison clothes that were removed in chapter forty-one.
Now Joseph gives new garments to every brother.
The man who was stripped now clothes the ones who stripped him.
The Cup that was taken is now given.
And to Benjamin, five changes.
Five portions again.
The favoritism pattern, but now openly, without fear of jealousy.
Because the brothers have changed.
The test is over.
They passed.
The Cup of favoritism no longer divides because the hearts that would have divided have been broken and rebuilt.
He sent to his father:
ten donkeys loaded with the good things of Egypt,
and ten female donkeys loaded with grain and bread and provision for his father by the way.
Ten donkeys.
Ten female donkeys.
Twenty animals loaded with the wealth of Egypt.
The father who left home with a staff and a stone pillow is now receiving twenty loads of provision from the son he thought was dead.
The Cup that was carried out of Canaan as a dream is now carried back to Canaan as grain and bread and the good of Egypt.
So he sent his brothers away, and they departed.
And he said to them:
See that you do not quarrel on the way.
Do not quarrel on the way.
do not be agitated on the road.
Joseph knows they will blame each other.
The confession of guilt in chapter forty-two.
The fear in chapter forty-three.
The tearing of clothes in chapter forty-four.
The brothers will be replaying every sin on the road home.
Joseph says: Do not.
The Cup is open.
Walk home in it.
The journey back should not be filled with recrimination.
The truth has been spoken.
The forgiveness has been given.
The reconciliation has happened.
Walk in it.
They went up out of Egypt and came into the land of Canaan,
to Jacob their father.
They told him, saying: Joseph is still alive.
He is ruler over all the land of Egypt.
Joseph is still alive.
The words that break twenty-two years of grief.
The son who was torn by wild animals.
The coat that was dipped in goat's blood.
The father who refused comfort.
The brothers who lied.
All of it, overturned by five words: Joseph is still alive.
His heart fainted, for he did not believe them.
his heart went numb.
Cold.
The Cup of grief, held for twenty-two years,
deepened by a blood-stained coat, confirmed by ten sons who lied,
is so deep that truth cannot reach it immediately.
The father who was deceived by a coat is now being told the opposite of what the coat proved.
And he cannot believe it.
The deception was too thorough.
The grief was too long.
The wound is too deep for sudden healing.
They told him all the words of Joseph which he had said to them.
When he saw the wagons which Joseph had sent to carry him,
the spirit of Jacob their father revived.
The spirit revived.
the spirit came alive.
Not by proof.
By wagons.
By the tangible evidence that the son he mourned is sending transport to bring him home.
The father who said I shall go down to Sheol to my son,
mourning,
now has his spirit revived by the son he thought was in Sheol.
The Cup of grief that held for twenty-two years finally lifts.
Not by argument.
Not by explanation.
By wagons sent by a living son.
The Cup that was emptied by a blood-stained coat is now refilled by the sight of transport sent by a living hand.
Israel said: It is enough.
Joseph, my son, is still alive.
I will go and see him before I die..enough.
The same word Jacob used when he said I have enough after Esau's reconciliation,
But here it is deeper.
Enough means: the grief is over.
The waiting is over.
The coat of blood is answered.
The lie is exposed.
The truth is here.
My son is alive.
The Cup that held grief for twenty two years is now poured out in three words:
it is enough.
The father who said all these things are against me now says:
it is enough.
The man who saw only loss now sees only life.
I will go and see him before I die.
The father who sent his son to check on his brothers will now go to the son.
The man who held the Cup of the covenant through every descent,
the dreaming, the labor, the wrestling, the limp,
the betrayal of his sons, the death of Rachel,
the silence after Shechem, will now carry the Cup into Egypt.
Not as a slave.
Not as a prisoner.
As a father going to see his son.
The four-hundred-year prophecy from chapter fifteen is fully in motion.
Your offspring will be sojourners in a land not theirs.
God told Abraham.
Now Jacob goes down to Egypt, not as a slave,
but as a father going to his son.
The descent that will become bondage begins as a family reunion.
The Cup that enters Egypt as a gift of grace will become the Cup that Egypt turns into a chain.
But that is later.
For now, the Cup overflows.
The brothers are reconciled.
The father is revived.
The wagons are loaded.
The covenant family is about to enter the land that will hold them for four hundred years.
The Cup that was sold for silver is now the Cup that saves a family.
The Cup that was thrown into a pit is now the Cup that feeds the world.
The Cup that was stripped of four garments is now the Cup that clothes every brother.
The Cup that was forgotten by a cup-bearer is now the Cup that revives a father's spirit.
The Cup that held tears for twenty-two years has now overflowed,
into reconciliation, into forgiveness, into a family restored, into a nation's beginning.
The dream was real.
The betrayal was real.
The waiting was real.
The providence was real.
The tears were real.
The reunion is real.
The Cup holds all of it, the pit and the palace,
the prison and the provision, the coat and the robes,
the silver and the tears.
The same Cup.
Seen from different ends.
Poured by the same God who said: I will be with you.
